meta.what: Figures that exist only on the Moon or Mars, for the 16 lunar regions (moon_cards.json) and the 57 Mars sites (mars_sites.json). Nothing already on those cards is repeated; links point to it.
meta.how_to_rerun: uv run python scripts/build_planet_factors.py   (add --offline to use saved files only)

kinds.measured: read from an orbital map at the site's coordinates; a map pixel or bin, never a measurement on the ground at the landing point (see scope)
kinds.model: a model value (e.g. the Mars Climate Database)
kinds.published figure: a number or sentence copied from a saved NASA page or paper
kinds.null: no figure; the note says why

meta.value_text: Where a published source gives words or a range instead of one number, value is null or a [low, high] pair and value_text holds the words to show.
meta.raw_folder: data/raw/planet_factors (every download logged in a _downloads.tsv beside it)

factors.name: Thermal inertia
factors.what_it_is: How strongly the top few centimetres of ground resist heating and cooling. Loose dust is low (below about 100), sand and crusted soil middle, rock and ice-cemented ground high.

factors.name: Near-surface hydrogen or water
factors.what_it_is: Hydrogen in the top tens of centimetres to about a metre, seen from orbit by the neutrons or gamma rays the ground gives off. Moon: hydrogen in ppm by weight. Mars: the same signal expressed as water (H2O) in weight per cent.
factors.unit: Moon: ppm H by weight; Mars: weight % H2O

connecting-ridge.source: Lunar Prospector neutron spectrometer, 'Hydrogen_halfdeg' (Feldman et al. 2001), PDS Geosciences Node
connecting-ridge.note: Half-degree bin holding the region centre; 264 bins centred inside the region range 143.8 to 147.4 ppm. The instrument's footprint is tens of kilometres, much wider than a half-degree bin near the pole, so this is a regional value, not a measurement at the landing point. It cannot tell ice in a cold trap from hydrogen spread through the soil.
connecting-ridge.scope: regional (orbital neutron footprint of tens of km)

factors.name: Quakes
factors.what_it_is: Ground shaking from inside the planet. Moon: shallow moonquakes from faults as the Moon cools and shrinks. Mars: marsquakes heard by NASA's InSight lander (2018-2022).

connecting-ridge.source: NASA release, 25 January 2024 (Watters et al. 2024, Planetary Science Journal)
connecting-ridge.note: The strongest shallow moonquake recorded by the Apollo seismometers (1969-1977) had its epicentre in the south-polar region, but its exact place could not be fixed; the cloud of possible epicentres covers many Artemis III candidate regions. Young thrust-fault scarps lie near and inside some of them. No count or rate is published for this region; no seismometer has worked near the south pole.
